title: Die Geschenke des kleinen Volkes
titleEn: The Gifts of the Little Folk
part: The Gifts of the Little Folk
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 182. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, schloß, ward, Kreiß).
about: A tailor and a hunchbacked goldsmith stumble on the little folk dancing by night, and both come away with the same strange parting gifts: their beards and hair shaved off, and a lump of coal apiece. What the contented tailor and the greedy goldsmith each make of that gift is the whole point of the tale. It follows a pattern common in the Grimm collection — two travellers, one encounter, two very different endings.

sentences.t: Ein Schneider und ein Goldschmied wanderten zusammen und vernahmen eines Abends, als die Sonne hinter die Berge gesunken war, den Klang einer fernen Musik, die immer deutlicher ward;
sentences.l: A tailor and a goldsmith were travelling together and heard one evening, when the sun had sunk behind the mountains, the sound of a distant music which grew ever more distinct;
sentences.i: A tailor and a goldsmith were journeying together, and one evening, when the sun had sunk behind the mountains, they caught the sound of a distant music that grew ever clearer;
sentences.n: vernehmen is an elevated word for catching a sound. ward is the older form of wurde: immer deutlicher ward — it kept growing clearer.

sentences.t: sie tönte ungewöhnlich aber so anmuthig, daß sie aller Müdigkeit vergaßen und rasch weiter schritten.
sentences.l: it sounded unusual but so charming that they forgot all their weariness and strode on quickly.
sentences.i: it had an uncommon sound, yet so sweet that they forgot how tired they were and strode quickly on.
sentences.n: anmuthig is the 1857 spelling of anmutig, graceful, charming. vergessen takes the genitive here — aller Müdigkeit. schritten is the past of schreiten, to stride; the shared entry gives the noun der Schritt, a step.

sentences.t: Der Mond war schon aufgestiegen, als sie zu einem Hügel gelangten, auf dem sie eine Menge kleiner Männer und Frauen erblickten, die sich bei den Händen gefaßt hatten, und mit größter Lust und Freudigkeit im Tanze herum wirbelten:
sentences.l: The moon had already risen when they reached a hill, on which they caught sight of a crowd of little men and women who had taken each other by the hands and were whirling round in the dance with the greatest pleasure and gladness:
sentences.i: The moon had already risen when they came to a hill, where they saw a crowd of little men and women who had joined hands and were whirling round in the dance with the greatest delight:
sentences.n: sich bei den Händen fassen — to take one another by the hands. Frauen here is simply the plural of Frau, women; the shared entry was written for an old genitive in a saint’s-day name.

sentences.t: sie sangen dazu auf das lieblichste;
sentences.l: they sang to it in the loveliest way;
sentences.i: and they sang to it most sweetly;
sentences.n: auf das lieblichste is the old adverbial superlative: in the loveliest manner.

sentences.t: und das war die Musik, die die Wanderer gehört hatten.
sentences.l: and that was the music which the travellers had heard.
sentences.n: die die is not a misprint: the first die is the relative pronoun standing for die Musik, the second is the article of die Wanderer, the subject inside the relative clause.

sentences.t: In der Mitte saß ein Alter, der etwas größer war als die übrigen, der einen buntfarbigen Rock trug, und dem ein eisgrauer Bart über die Brust herabhieng.
sentences.l: In the middle sat an old one who was somewhat bigger than the rest, who wore a motley coat, and from whom an iron-grey beard hung down over the breast.
sentences.i: In the middle sat an old man, somewhat taller than the rest, wearing a coat of many colours, with an iron-grey beard hanging down over his chest.
sentences.n: ein Alter is the adjective alt used as a noun, an old man; the shared entry for alter was written for its vocative use elsewhere. Three relative clauses hang off him in a row (der …, der …, dem …), the last with a dative of possession: the beard hangs down on him.

sentences.t: Die beiden blieben voll Verwunderung stehen und sahen dem Tanz zu.
sentences.l: The two stopped, full of astonishment, and looked on at the dance.
sentences.i: The two stood still in astonishment and watched the dance.
sentences.n: stehen bleiben, to stop; zusehen + dative, to look on at something. Both are separable, and both particles wait at the end.

sentences.t: Der Alte winkte, sie sollten eintreten, und das kleine Volk öffnete bereitwillig seinen Kreis.
sentences.l: The old man beckoned that they should step in, and the little folk readily opened its circle.
sentences.i: The old man beckoned them to step in, and the little folk readily opened their ring.
sentences.n: das kleine Volk is plain High German — the little folk of the title; the Low German label in the shared entry belongs to another tale. Volk is neuter singular, so German says seinen Kreis, its circle, where English wants a plural.

sentences.t: Der Goldschmied, der einen Höcker hatte und wie alle Buckeligen keck genug war, trat herzu:
sentences.l: The goldsmith, who had a hump and, like all hunchbacks, was bold enough, stepped up:
sentences.i: The goldsmith, who had a hump and was bold enough, as all hunchbacks are, stepped up to them:
sentences.n: wie alle Buckeligen is stated as a known fact — the 1857 text takes the boldness of hunchbacks for granted, and the end of the tale plays on it.

sentences.t: der Schneider empfand zuerst einige Scheu und hielt sich zurück, doch als er sah wie es so lustig hergieng, faßte er sich ein Herz und kam nach.
sentences.l: the tailor felt at first some shyness and held himself back, but when he saw how merrily it went there, he took himself a heart and came after.
sentences.i: the tailor felt some awe at first and hung back, but when he saw how merrily things were going, he took heart and followed.
sentences.n: die Scheu is the noun here, shyness or awe — the shared entry gives the adjective scheu. sich ein Herz fassen, to take heart; hergehen is used of goings-on: es gieng lustig her, things were going merrily.

sentences.t: Alsbald schloß sich der Kreiß wieder und die Kleinen sangen und tanzten in den wildesten Sprüngen weiter, der Alte aber nahm ein breites Messer, das an seinem Gürtel hieng, wetzte es und als es hinlänglich geschärft war, blickte er sich nach den Fremdlingen um.
sentences.l: At once the ring closed again and the little ones sang and danced on in the wildest leaps; the old man, however, took a broad knife that hung at his belt, whetted it, and when it was sufficiently sharpened he looked round after the strangers.
sentences.i: At once the ring closed again and the little ones went on singing and dancing in the wildest leaps; but the old man took a broad knife that hung at his belt, whetted it, and when it was sharp enough he looked round at the strangers.
sentences.n: Sprüngen is the dative plural of der Sprung, a leap — a High German noun, not the Low German verb form the shared entry gives. Kreiß is the 1857 spelling of Kreis, and schloß sich is the past of sich schließen, to close (the shared entry for schloß was written for das Schloß, a castle). sich umblicken: blickte sich … um.

sentences.t: Es ward ihnen angst, aber sie hatten nicht lange Zeit sich zu besinnen, der Alte packte den Goldschmied und schor in der größten Geschwindigkeit ihm Haupthaar und Bart glatt hinweg;
sentences.l: It became afraid to them, but they had not long time to collect themselves: the old man seized the goldsmith and sheared his head-hair and beard smooth away with the greatest speed;
sentences.i: Fear came over them, but they had no time to think: the old man seized the goldsmith and with the greatest speed sheared his hair and beard clean away;
sentences.n: es ward ihnen angst is impersonal with a dative — literally “it grew afraid to them”. sich besinnen is plain High German here, to collect one’s thoughts; the shared entry labels it Low German. hinweg scheren is separable: schor … hinweg.

sentences.t: ein gleiches geschah hierauf dem Schneider.
sentences.l: a like thing happened thereupon to the tailor.
sentences.i: the same then happened to the tailor.
sentences.n: ein gleiches — a like thing, the same; dem Schneider is the dative of the person it happens to.

sentences.t: Doch ihre Angst verschwand, als der Alte nach vollbrachter Arbeit beiden freundlich auf die Schulter klopfte, als wollte er sagen, sie hätten es gut gemacht daß sie ohne Sträuben Alles willig hätten geschehen lassen.
sentences.l: But their fear vanished when the old man, after the work was accomplished, patted them both kindly on the shoulder, as if he wanted to say they had done it well in letting everything happen willingly without resistance.
sentences.i: But their fear vanished when the old man, his work done, clapped them both kindly on the shoulder, as though he meant to say that they had done well to let it all happen willingly and without a struggle.
sentences.n: nach vollbrachter Arbeit is compressed: the work having been accomplished. hätten … gemacht and hätten geschehen lassen are subjunctive because the speech is only imagined, not spoken — the old man never says a word in the whole tale.

sentences.t: Er zeigte mit dem Finger auf einen Haufen Kohlen, der zur Seite lag, und deutete ihnen durch Gebärden an daß sie ihre Taschen damit füllen sollten.
sentences.l: He pointed with his finger at a heap of coals that lay to one side, and indicated to them by gestures that they should fill their pockets with them.
sentences.i: He pointed with his finger at a heap of coals lying to one side, and made signs to them that they should fill their pockets with it.
sentences.n: andeuten is separable: deutete … an, to indicate, hint at. durch Gebärden — by gestures, since he does not speak.

sentences.t: Beide gehorchten, obgleich sie nicht wußten wozu ihnen die Kohlen dienen sollten, und giengen dann weiter, um ein Nachtlager zu suchen.
sentences.l: Both obeyed, although they did not know what the coals were to serve them for, and then went on further to look for a night’s lodging.
sentences.i: Both obeyed, though they did not know what use the coals were to be to them, and then went on to look for a lodging for the night.
sentences.n: wozu — for what, to what end; the shared entry was written for a different use of the word. dienen takes a dative: ihnen dienen, to be of use to them.

sentences.t: Als sie ins Thal gekommen waren, schlug die Glocke des benachbarten Klosters zwölf Uhr:
sentences.l: When they had come into the valley, the bell of the neighbouring monastery struck twelve o’clock:
sentences.i: When they had come down into the valley, the bell of the nearby monastery struck twelve:
sentences.n: Thal is the 1857 spelling of Tal. Midnight is the hour at which such gatherings break off, and the colon runs straight into what follows.

sentences.t: augenblicklich verstummte der Gesang, Alles war verschwunden, und der Hügel lag in einsamem Mondschein.
sentences.l: instantly the singing fell silent, everything had vanished, and the hill lay in lonely moonlight.
sentences.i: in an instant the singing fell silent, everything had vanished, and the hill lay in lonely moonlight.
sentences.n: verstummen — to fall silent (stumm, mute). Alles is capitalised in 1857 where modern German writes alles.

sentences.t: Die beiden Wanderer fanden eine Herberge und deckten sich auf dem Strohlager mit ihren Röcken zu, vergaßen aber wegen ihrer Müdigkeit die Kohlen zuvor heraus zu nehmen.
sentences.l: The two travellers found an inn and covered themselves up on the straw bed with their coats, but forgot, on account of their weariness, to take the coals out beforehand.
sentences.i: The two travellers found a lodging and covered themselves with their coats on the straw bed, but were too weary to remember to take the coals out first.
sentences.n: zudecken is separable: deckten sich … zu. heraus nehmen is separable too, and 1857 prints it as two words.

sentences.t: Ein schwerer Druck auf ihren Gliedern weckte sie früher als gewöhnlich.
sentences.l: A heavy pressure on their limbs woke them earlier than usual.
sentences.n: der Druck, the pressure or weight — the gold is felt before it is seen.

sentences.t: Sie griffen in die Taschen und wollten ihren Augen nicht trauen, als sie sahen daß sie nicht mit Kohlen, sondern mit reinem Gold angefüllt waren;
sentences.l: They reached into their pockets and would not trust their eyes when they saw that they were filled not with coals but with pure gold;
sentences.i: They reached into their pockets and could not believe their eyes when they saw that they were filled not with coals but with pure gold;
sentences.n: trauen takes the dative — ihren Augen trauen, to trust one’s eyes; the shared entry gives the other trauen, to marry a couple. nicht … sondern: not … but rather.

sentences.t: auch Haupthaar und Bart war glücklich wieder in aller Fülle vorhanden.
sentences.l: head-hair and beard too were happily there again in all their fullness.
sentences.i: their hair and beards, too, were happily back again in full.
sentences.n: vorhanden sein — to be there, to be at hand. The verb stays singular after the paired subject, as 1857 German often lets it.

sentences.t: Sie waren nun reiche Leute geworden, doch besaß der Goldschmied, der seiner habgierigen Natur gemäß die Taschen besser gefüllt hatte, nocheinmal so viel als der Schneider.
sentences.l: They had now become rich people, but the goldsmith, who in keeping with his greedy nature had filled his pockets better, possessed once again as much as the tailor.
sentences.i: They were rich men now; but the goldsmith, who true to his greedy nature had filled his pockets better, had twice as much as the tailor.
sentences.n: nocheinmal so viel — literally “once again as much”, that is, twice as much. reiche is the adjective rich here; the shared entry for reiche was written for the verb reichen, to hand. seiner Natur gemäß takes the dative: in accordance with his nature.

sentences.t: Ein Habgieriger, wenn er viel hat, verlangt noch mehr, der Goldschmied machte dem Schneider den Vorschlag, noch einen Tag zu verweilen, am Abend wieder hinaus zu gehen, um sich bei dem Alten auf dem Berge noch größere Schätze zu holen.
sentences.l: A greedy man, when he has much, demands still more: the goldsmith made the tailor the proposal to tarry one more day, to go out again in the evening, in order to fetch himself still greater treasures from the old man on the mountain.
sentences.i: A greedy man, having much, wants more still: the goldsmith proposed to the tailor that they stay another day and go out again in the evening, to fetch themselves still greater treasures from the old man on the hill.
sentences.n: Ein Habgieriger is an adjective used as a noun, a greedy one; the sentence stands as a general saying before the story goes on. verlangt is present tense here, not the past participle the shared entry describes.

sentences.t: Der Schneider wollte nicht und sagte „ich habe genug und bin zufrieden:
sentences.l: The tailor did not want to and said “I have enough and am content:
sentences.i: The tailor would not, and said, “I have enough and am content:
sentences.n: wollte nicht stands alone: the infinitive (gehen) is simply left out after the modal, as German may do.

sentences.t: jetzt werde ich Meister, heirathe meinen angenehmen Gegenstand (wie er seine Liebste nannte) und bin ein glücklicher Mann.“
sentences.l: now I become a master, marry my agreeable object (as he called his sweetheart) and am a happy man.”
sentences.i: now I shall become a master, marry my agreeable object (as he called his sweetheart), and be a happy man.”
sentences.n: The round brackets are the Grimms’ own aside to the reader, printed inside the tailor’s speech. Meister werden is to rise from journeyman to guild master — the point at which a craftsman may set up his own shop and marry. mein angenehmer Gegenstand is stiff, book-learnt gallantry, and is meant to raise a smile.

sentences.t: Doch wollte er, ihm zu Gefallen, den Tag noch bleiben.
sentences.l: Yet he wanted, as a favour to him, to stay the day still.
sentences.i: Still, to oblige him, he was willing to stay the day out.
sentences.n: jemandem zu Gefallen — to please someone, as a favour to him; der Gefallen here is the noun, a favour, not the past participle of fallen that the shared entry gives.

sentences.t: Abends hieng der Goldschmied noch ein paar Taschen über die Schulter, um recht einsacken zu können, und machte sich auf den Weg zu dem Hügel.
sentences.l: In the evening the goldsmith hung a couple more bags over his shoulder, in order to be able to sack things up properly, and made his way to the hill.
sentences.i: In the evening the goldsmith slung a couple more bags over his shoulder so that he could really pack it in, and set off for the hill.
sentences.n: hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing. einsacken, to put into a sack, is a plain greedy word; recht here means thoroughly, properly.

sentences.t: Er fand, wie in der vorigen Nacht, das kleine Volk bei Gesang und Tanz, der Alte schor ihn abermals glatt und deutete ihm an Kohlen mitzunehmen.
sentences.l: He found, as on the previous night, the little folk at song and dance; the old man sheared him smooth once again and indicated to him to take coals along.
sentences.i: He found the little folk at their singing and dancing, just as on the night before; the old man sheared him clean again and made signs to him to take coals with him.
sentences.n: bei Gesang und Tanz — at their singing and dancing. andeuten and mitnehmen are both separable: deutete … an, mit zu nehmen.

sentences.t: Er zögerte nicht einzustecken was nur in seine Taschen gehen wollte, kehrte ganz glückselig heim und deckte sich mit dem Rock zu.
sentences.l: He did not hesitate to pocket whatever would only go into his pockets, returned home quite blissful and covered himself up with his coat.
sentences.i: He did not hesitate to stuff in whatever his pockets would hold, went home in bliss, and covered himself with his coat.
sentences.n: heimkehren is separable: kehrte … heim, returned home; the shared entry for kehrte was written for zukehren, to turn towards. was nur … gehen wollte — whatever would go in at all.

sentences.t: „Wenn das Gold auch drückt,“ sprach er, „ich will das schon ertragen,“ und schlief endlich mit dem süßen Vorgefühl ein, Morgen als steinreicher Mann zu erwachen.
sentences.l: “Even if the gold presses,” spoke he, “I will bear that well enough,” and fell asleep at last with the sweet foretaste of waking tomorrow as a stone-rich man.
sentences.i: “Even if the gold weighs on me,” he said, “I shall bear it well enough” — and fell asleep at last with the sweet foretaste of waking in the morning a man of enormous wealth.
sentences.n: drücken here is to press, to weigh on someone; the shared entry gives the idiom ein Auge zudrücken. schon in ich will das schon ertragen is the particle of confidence: well enough, never fear. steinreich, ‘stone-rich’, is ordinary German for immensely rich.

sentences.t: Als er die Augen öffnete, erhob er sich schnell, um die Taschen zu untersuchen, aber wie erstaunte er als er nichts herauszog als schwarze Kohlen, er mochte so oft hinein greifen als er wollte.
sentences.l: When he opened his eyes he raised himself quickly in order to examine the pockets, but how he was astonished when he drew out nothing but black coals, reach into them as often as he might.
sentences.i: When he opened his eyes he got up quickly to search his pockets, but how astonished he was to draw out nothing but black coals, reach in as often as he liked.
sentences.n: er mochte … als er wollte is a concessive without a conjunction: reach in as often as he might. herausziehen is separable, printed here as one word: herauszog.

sentences.t: „Noch bleibt mir das Gold, das ich die Nacht vorher gewonnen habe“ dachte er und holte es herbei, aber wie erschrack er, als er sah daß es ebenfalls wieder zu Kohle geworden war.
sentences.l: “The gold that I won the night before still remains to me,” thought he, and fetched it out, but how he took fright when he saw that it too had become coal again.
sentences.i: “I still have the gold I won the night before,” he thought, and fetched it out; but how he took fright when he saw that it too had turned back to coal.
sentences.n: bleibt mir is a dative of possession — it remains to me, I still have it. erschrack (1857 for erschrak) is the intransitive verb, to take fright.

sentences.t: Er schlug sich mit der schwarzbestäubten Hand an die Stirne, da fühlte er daß der ganze Kopf kahl und glatt war wie der Bart.
sentences.l: He struck himself with the coal-dusted hand on the forehead; then he felt that the whole head was bald and smooth like the beard.
sentences.i: He struck his forehead with his coal-dusted hand — and felt that his whole head was as bald and smooth as his chin.
sentences.n: sich an die Stirne schlagen: the person struck is folded into the reflexive sich, so German needs no possessive. Stirne keeps the old final -e.

sentences.t: Aber sein Misgeschick war noch nicht zu Ende, er merkte erst jetzt daß ihm zu dem Höcker auf dem Rücken noch ein zweiter eben so großer vorn auf der Brust gewachsen war.
sentences.l: But his ill luck was not yet at an end: only now did he notice that, to the hump on his back, a second just as big had grown on him in front on the breast.
sentences.i: But his ill luck was not over yet: only now did he notice that, besides the hump on his back, a second just as large had grown on him in front, on his chest.
sentences.n: erst jetzt — only now. ihm is again the dative of the person a thing happens to: it grew on him. Misgeschick is the 1857 spelling of Missgeschick.

sentences.t: Da erkannte er die Strafe seiner Habgier und begann laut zu weinen.
sentences.l: Then he recognised the punishment of his greed and began to weep aloud.
sentences.i: Then he knew it for the punishment of his greed, and began to weep aloud.
sentences.n: die Strafe seiner Habgier — the punishment for his greed, put as a plain genitive.

sentences.t: Der gute Schneider, der davon aufgeweckt ward, tröstete den Unglücklichen so gut es gehen wollte und sprach „du bist mein Geselle auf der Wanderschaft gewesen, du sollst bei mir bleiben und mit von meinem Schatz zehren.“
sentences.l: The good tailor, who was woken by it, comforted the unfortunate man as well as it would go and spoke “you have been my companion on the journeying, you shall stay with me and live along off my treasure.”
sentences.i: The good tailor, woken by the noise, comforted the poor wretch as best he could, and said, “You have been my fellow on the road; you shall stay with me and live with me off my treasure.”
sentences.n: so gut es gehen wollte — as well as it would go, as best he could. mit … zehren: to live off something along with someone, the mit standing well away from its verb.

sentences.t: Er hielt Wort, aber der arme Goldschmied mußte sein Lebtag die beiden Höcker tragen und seinen kahlen Kopf mit einer Mütze bedecken.
sentences.l: He kept word, but the poor goldsmith had to carry the two humps his whole life long and cover his bald head with a cap.
sentences.i: He kept his word; but the poor goldsmith had to carry the two humps all his life, and cover his bald head with a cap.
sentences.n: Wort halten — to keep one’s word, with no article. sein Lebtag is an old fixed accusative: all his life long. The tale ends with the punishment left standing and not undone.

glossary.alter: alt — old; used as a noun, ein Alter = an old man
glossary.besinnen: sich besinnen — to collect one’s thoughts, reflect (plain High German here)
glossary.deckten: zudecken — covered up (3rd pl. past; separable zu-: deckten sich … zu)
glossary.frauen: die Frau — women (gen. pl. here: kleiner Männer und Frauen)
glossary.gefallen: der Gefallen — favour (jemandem zu Gefallen: to please someone, as a favour to him)
glossary.heirathe: heirathen — (I) marry (1st sg. present; 1857 spelling of heiraten), not a subjunctive of reported speech
glossary.kehrte: heimkehren — returned home (3rd sg. past; separable heim: kehrte … heim)
glossary.klang: der Klang — sound, ring (acc. sg.; from klingen, to sound), not the past of klingen
glossary.reiche: reich — rich (inflected; reiche Leute: rich people)
glossary.scheu: die Scheu — shyness, awe, diffidence (noun; einige Scheu empfinden: to feel some awe)
glossary.schloß: schließen — closed (3rd sg. past; sich schließen: to close again), not das Schloß, a castle
glossary.schritten: schreiten — strode (3rd pl. past; weiter schreiten: to stride on), not der Schritt, a step
glossary.sprüngen: der Sprung — leap, bound (dat. pl.; in den wildesten Sprüngen: in the wildest leaps) — High German noun, not a Low German verb
glossary.trauen: trauen — to trust (+ dative; seinen Augen trauen: to trust one’s eyes)
glossary.volk: das Volk — folk, people (das kleine Volk: the little folk, the elves) — plain High German
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (not the adverb weg, away)
glossary.werde: werden — (I) become, shall become (1st sg. present; jetzt werde ich Meister), not the subjunctive of reported speech
glossary.wozu: wozu — for what, to what end
